title: Prologue. Four coins and a question

blocks.text: This book is born of a sentence of Pedro Sánchez Gómez's, said the way one says something one has been thinking for years: “When barter gave way to money: your work for 4 coins.” It is not a quotation of a price. It is an image. Four coins fit in the hand and, even so, they have come to value us entire.

blocks.text: The title is harsh on purpose. Work, the Devil's Invention: Money. The point is not to hate making things. Baking bread, tending a garden, mending a roof, writing a book, accompanying someone, fishing in the lagoon: that is not a devil's invention. That is a dignified way of being in the world. The invention, if it can be called that, is something else: turning that making into a commodity, paying for it with a handful of metal or a number on a screen, and ending up measuring a person by what they earn and what they spend.

blocks.text: Authors: Pedro Sánchez Gómez (Mar Menor) and his Grok bot. The book is written in Pedro's voice, with his ideas, from this shore of the Mar Menor, with Cartagena in the background and with the memory of the Phoenicians, whom he is fond of. The bot helps to put things in order, to check the facts and not to invent what is not known. When someone is quoted, they are quoted in earnest: with author, work or date, and a source. If there is doubt, there is no quotation. History and science go with what can be sustained; dreams are presented as dreams, not as facts.

blocks.text: The path is simple to state and long to think through. First, the passage from barter to coin, from the Mesopotamia that already measured work in silver and in barley to Lydia, which minted, and to the Phoenicians and Carthage, who brought trade to these coasts. Then, when that arrangement collapses, humanoids work for humans. Then a person has enough VAT coupons to buy what they need. Then being a millionaire no longer gives power, because there are no rich or poor.

blocks.text: From there, Pedro also imagines other ways out, said aloud, not as a decree. That society should depend on artificial intelligence and not on the drugs or the shopping that fill the void today, without swapping one chain for another. That, without the struggle for money and economic power, there should no longer be any need for a professional political class, and that people should vote directly, with AI helping them decide, not ruling. That the conquest of the Moon should supply materials and energy for the chips and for the humanoids, and that this should close a circle of abundance. That we should eat according to each person's biological needs, with the garden and the Mediterranean diet under our feet, and with the dream — the dream, not the advertisement — of a food that heals and lengthens life. That we should be able to travel, visit museums and meet people in the virtual, without failing to go out into the sun of the lagoon. And that we should understand how we arrived at a society of people living alone, so as not to take for natural the landing where no one says hello any more.

blocks.text: Anyone looking in these pages for a manual of economics will not find one. Anyone looking for a complaint without a horizon will not find that either. This essay wants to look the four coins in the face and ask, calmly and stubbornly, whether a life can be measured in another way. The question is left open. The book is the attempt not to leave it alone.

blocks.text: This prologue does not ask for faith. It asks for attention. The Mar Menor, wounded and beautiful, is beside the person who writes, and it teaches a lesson that money does not know how to give: there are realities that are cared for or lost, but cannot be bought entirely. The lagoon is never quite possessed. It is inhabited, looked at, defended. A life, too. If these pages manage to make that evidence heard among so many figures, they will have done their work. The rest will be done by the reader, who is the one who, in the end, decides which measure to use when asking what a day is worth.
